Topical corticosteroids are used by ophthalmolo- gists in herpes simplex keratitis but always under appropriate an- tiviral cover and their use requires considerable experience. They should never be given for an undiagnosed red eye and many con- sultant ophthalmic surgeons believe that general practitioners should never begin therapy without an ophthalmic opinion. 1494 Corticosteroids Further studies and discussions on the inappropriate use of corti- costeroids to treat eye disorders are listed below.2-10 1. Use of corticosteroids in combination with antimicrobial drugs in the treatment of infectious corneal disease. Ophthalmology 1991; 98: 847–53. Intranasal administration. Local adverse effects from intra- nasal corticosteroids include irritation, epistaxis, and smell and taste disturbances (see also above). Ulceration, septal perfora- tion, and hypersensitivity reactions have occurred.1 There have been cases of Cushing’s syndrome associated with inappropriately prolonged use of corticosteroid nasal drops in children.2,3 Such drops should not be prescribed on a repeat pre- scription basis; where treatment is contemplated for more than 6 weeks appropriate monitoring has been recommended. See also Adrenal Suppression, under Adverse Effects, above. 1. Salib RJ, Howarth PH.
